name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,838

entries.clue: Tennis champion Chris referring to team from another sport (7)

blocks.note: Chris Evert won eighteen grand slam singles titles in the 1970s and 80s
a book on tennis is a book referring to it

annotation.surface: A tennis champion getting a mention from a side that plays something else.
annotation.walkthrough: Everton are a Liverpool football club, and they run through the whole grid: the puzzle appeared on the day of the last league game at their old ground.
annotation.definitionFit: Everton are a football team, so 'another sport' is the step off the tennis court that the champion's surname has just set up.

entries.clue: Great desires, though not at first, for income (8)

indicatorNotes.though not at first: 'not at first' strikes out whatever stands at the front, so the word named loses its opening letter

blocks.note: desires felt keenly are yearnings
the letter standing at the head of that word is the one struck off

annotation.surface: Grand ambitions that were not there at the start, set against what actually comes in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Great' is not a piece of its own: it belongs with 'desires', since yearnings are already desires of the strong kind. Beheadings are signalled by words of position — first, head, top.
annotation.definitionFit: Earnings are the money work brings in, the wage-and-salary half of income rather than rent or interest.

entries.clue: Mile End’s poetic evening (3)

indicatorNotes.’s: the possessive says the letters belong to the words in front of it, sitting inside them unbroken

blocks.note: the run begins inside the first word and finishes inside the second

annotation.surface: Evening coming down over Mile End, put in a poet's diction.
annotation.walkthrough: Mile End is a district of London's East End, so the capitals read as a place name doing place-name work. The apostrophe is the entire instruction — setters rarely let a hidden word off this lightly.
annotation.definitionFit: E'en is the poets' clipped form of evening, the apostrophe standing in for the letters dropped to keep a line scanning.

entries.clue: Hearing about boredom, leaving university at regular intervals (9)

annotation.definitionNote: Triennial is an adjective and 'at regular intervals' is an adverbial phrase; the setter defines by the pattern the word describes rather than by a word that would slot into a sentence in its place.

indicatorNotes.about: letters put about something are wrapped round it, part in front and part behind
indicatorNotes.leaving: what leaves has gone from where it was, so the letter named after it drops out

blocks.note: a hearing in court is a trial
ennui is boredom of the listless, world-weary kind
u = university, and this is the letter that leaves

annotation.surface: A hearing into boredom, which the university keeps walking out of at fixed intervals.
annotation.walkthrough: The outer word splits four letters in, which is where the difficulty sits — containers usually open at a joint the eye can find. Ennui came over from French and keeps its run of vowels.
annotation.definitionFit: Something triennial happens every three years, one regular interval; the clue names the pattern rather than the number.

entries.clue: Denial country’s welcoming for example (8)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: a host welcoming someone takes them in, so the letters named before it open up to admit what follows

blocks.note: a country is a nation
for example is written eg

annotation.surface: A country's welcome, held up as an instance of saying no.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For example' has a two-letter spelling, eg, and setters drop it into wordplay as freely as they use 'say'. The definition is the lone first word, doing none of the surface's work.
annotation.definitionFit: A negation is a denial — the act of saying that something is not so, in logic or in plain argument.

entries.clue: Small amount I included in total for sports arena (7)

indicatorNotes.included in: what is included in something sits inside it, so the letters named first go within the word named after

blocks.note: the total of a column of figures is its sum
a tad is a small amount
the clue's own pronoun, taken as a letter

annotation.surface: Someone adding a small amount of their own money into the total.
annotation.walkthrough: This answer and 1 across together name the ground Everton moved to, which is what makes 15 across's 'home to be left' the news of the day. 'Tad' is worth keeping: always a small amount.
annotation.definitionFit: A stadium is the banked arena a crowd watches sport in, the general word covering grounds, bowls and tracks alike.

entries.clue: Low point, bad, see suffering (6)

indicatorNotes.suffering: something suffering is in a bad way, out of sorts, and letters out of sorts are letters in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: A low moment in someone's life: things are bad, and the suffering shows.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Low point' sounds on the surface like a bad patch in a life, and in the answer it is a physical depth. Anagram fodder rarely arrives as plainly comma-separated as this.
annotation.definitionFit: The seabed is the floor of the ocean, the lowest point there is once you are under water.

entries.clue: A temptation, we hear, to diminish (5)

indicatorNotes.we hear: we hear tells you to trust the sound of the word named, not the way it is written

blocks.note: the clue's opening article, taken as a letter
what is dangled to tempt a fish is bait, and that sound is spelt this way here

annotation.surface: A temptation which, by all reports, is fading away.
annotation.walkthrough: The leading A is the answer's first letter and nothing more, a trick setters use constantly and one that reads far too easily as part of the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To abate is to diminish: a storm abates, a nuisance is abated, the force of the thing drops away.

entries.clue: Anger as country’s land taken away (3)

indicatorNotes.taken away: what is taken away is gone altogether, so the letters named just before it come out of the word they sit in

blocks.note: the country on the far side of the Irish Sea
these four letters are the ones removed, and they sit at the end of that country's name

annotation.surface: Fury at a country having its territory confiscated.
annotation.walkthrough: The deletion is a whole word hiding inside a longer one, which you see the moment you stop reading 'land' as scenery. Ire is the crossword's short, useful word for anger.
annotation.definitionFit: Ire is anger in its formal or literary dress — to draw someone's ire is to make them furious.

entries.clue: Confused situation in Timor, as shown (6)

indicatorNotes.in: in says the letters wanted are inside the words that follow, not something those words mean

blocks.note: the run starts partway through the first word and carries straight on through the next two

annotation.surface: A tangled state of affairs in Timor, as the reports showed.
annotation.walkthrough: Hidden words live off their punctuation: this run crosses both gaps and a comma, which is exactly what stops the eye. A morass was a literal swamp long before it was a mess.
annotation.definitionFit: A morass is a tangle you cannot get clear of, the figurative sense of a swamp that swallows whatever steps into it.

entries.clue: Called about family’s position on scale (7)

indicatorNotes.about: letters put about something are wrapped round it, one part in front and one behind

blocks.note: called on the telephone is rang
your kin are your family

annotation.surface: A phone call about where the family stands.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Called' is the telephone's past tense here, not a name or a summons, and that is the whole disguise. Kin for family is a staple worth learning in both directions.
annotation.definitionFit: A ranking is the place something holds on a scale: second in the ranking is second on the list.

entries.clue: A friend, pure at heart, not seeking reward (7)

indicatorNotes.at heart: the heart of a word is its middle, so what is wanted is the letters at the centre of the word named

blocks.note: the clue's own article, taken as a letter
a mate is a friend
the two letters at the centre of that four-letter word

annotation.surface: A friend who is pure at heart and wants nothing back for it.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the moral-sounding tail of the sentence, which reads as more praise for the friend. 'At heart' is reliable: it always points at a word's middle letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An amateur plays or paints unpaid, for the love of it, and taking no reward is exactly what separates one from a professional.

entries.clue: Initially flippant, unpredictable, entering pub as a joke (2,3)

indicatorNotes.Initially: initially asks for what comes first, so each word named gives up only its opening letter
indicatorNotes.entering: whatever enters a place goes inside it, so those letters drop into the middle of the word that follows

blocks.note: a pub is an inn
the opening letters of the two words, in the order given

annotation.surface: Someone flippant and unpredictable walking into a pub and meaning none of it seriously.
annotation.walkthrough: Two initials and a three-letter pub is a lot of machinery for five letters, which is why the enumeration matters: (2,3) tells you a phrase is wanted before you have a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To do something in fun is to do it as a joke, meaning no harm by it — the phrase that follows an apology.

entries.clue: Big fort redeveloped as a plant (7)

indicatorNotes.redeveloped: a site redeveloped is pulled down and put back differently, and the letters named are put back the same way

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: A large fort being redeveloped into something green.
annotation.walkthrough: Frogbit is a floating pond plant with small round leaves, common in English ditches and rarely met outside them. The fodder sits right against its indicator, which is the tell.
annotation.definitionFit: Frogbit is a small floating water plant of still ponds and ditches, so the bare 'a plant' is the plain botanical sense.

entries.clue: Article by writer, lower in rank — not how to describe this puzzle! (9)

annotation.definition: not how to describe this puzzle!

blocks.note: the definite article
the setter writing the clue means himself
less means lower in amount or standing

annotation.surface: An article and its writer, marked down the pecking order.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition works by denial: Everton run through this grid from 1 across to 32, so the one thing the puzzle is not is without a subject. 'Me' for writer is the setter's standard self-reference.
annotation.definitionFit: A themeless puzzle has no linking subject, and this one is Everton end to end — so the setter defines the word by saying it does not apply.

entries.clue: In from France half-heartedly interfere with honour (7)

indicatorNotes.half-heartedly: the heart of the word is halved — the doubled letter at its centre is left standing only once

blocks.note: in translated into French is en, which naming the country asks for
to nobble a horse or a juror is to interfere with it
the pair of letters at that word's heart is cut to one, and this is the one that goes

annotation.surface: Someone over from France getting half-heartedly in the way of an honour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half-heartedly' is precise rather than vague: the heart of NOBBLE is a doubled letter, and half of a double is one of it. French en turns up whenever a clue mentions France or Paris.
annotation.definitionFit: To ennoble someone is to honour them — literally by making them a noble, and by extension by raising them in anyone's eyes.

entries.clue: Well-behaved child I hugged as home to be left for 1A/5D (8)

indicatorNotes.hugged: whoever is hugged is wrapped up by the arms either side, so the letter named sits between the two pieces

blocks.note: a well-behaved child is a good one
the clue's own pronoun, taken as a letter
a son is somebody's child

annotation.surface: A parent remembering hugging a well-behaved child in a house they are about to leave.
annotation.walkthrough: Goodison Park was Everton's ground for 133 years, and this puzzle ran on the day of the last league game there. The cross-reference is misprinted: the new stadium is 1 across and 5 across.
annotation.definitionFit: Goodison Park is the Liverpool ground Everton played on until 2025, the home they left for the new stadium named at 1 and 5 across.

entries.clue: “Dixie” - part of side, a natural (4)

indicatorNotes.part of: part of a thing is a piece taken from inside it, so the letters wanted sit unbroken within the words that follow

blocks.note: the run picks up inside the first word and finishes inside the last

annotation.surface: Dixie, one of the side, and a born talent.
annotation.walkthrough: Dixie Dean scored sixty league goals for Everton in 1927-28, a record nobody has come near since, so 'a natural' is a tribute rather than padding.
annotation.definitionFit: Dixie was the nickname of Everton's William Ralph Dean, so the name in quotation marks points straight at the surname it came attached to.

entries.clue: Official rearranged exams — nice (9)

indicatorNotes.rearranged: a room rearranged holds the same furniture in a new order, which is what happens to these letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: An official who shifted the exam timetable around, which was decent of him.
annotation.walkthrough: An exciseman collected the duty on spirits, tobacco and tea, and was the least welcome official in Georgian Britain; Robert Burns did the job for the last years of his life.
annotation.definitionFit: An exciseman is the government officer who collects excise duty on goods, so 'official' is his plain job description.

entries.clue: Something to help finding place — make reservation with Antony, say (8)

indicatorNotes.say: say marks what stands before it as one instance of something, so a name is offered as an example rather than for itself

blocks.note: to book a table is to make a reservation
Mark Antony, Caesar's lieutenant, is one man who carried that first name

annotation.surface: Advice on finding somewhere: reserve it, and bring Antony.
annotation.walkthrough: A bookmark is as often a saved web address now as a ribbon in a novel, and either keeps your place. Everything after the dash is instruction; the phrase in front of it defines.
annotation.definitionFit: A bookmark holds the page you stopped at so you can find your place again — ribbon, card or saved link alike.

entries.clue: Friend welcoming media boss is in Paris giving support (8)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: someone welcoming takes a visitor indoors, so the letters named first open to let the rest inside

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
the boss of a newspaper is its editor, shortened to ed
in Paris they say est for is, and naming the city names the language wanted

annotation.surface: A friend welcoming a newspaper editor who happens to be over in Paris.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' is the standard way of asking for French, and it asks one small word at a time — est, et, rue, ami. To put someone on a pedestal is to admire them past the point of sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the block a statue or a column stands on, so it supports whatever has been set above it.

entries.clue: 1966 World Cup winner Alan’s essential for the game (4)

blocks.note: the youngest man in England's winning side that July, and an Everton championship midfielder soon after
no match of any code starts until this is out on the pitch

annotation.surface: A World Cup winner named Alan who is indispensable to the game.
annotation.walkthrough: England won the 1966 final at Wembley and this player joined Everton the following month, winning the league with them in 1970. Two definitions of four letters is about as short as a clue gets.
annotation.definitionFit: Alan Ball wore number seven in the 1966 final, so the surname answers the description; and the ball itself is the one thing no game can be played without.

entries.clue: Unusually brief, cold, mostly convincing (8)

indicatorNotes.Unusually: what is unusual is out of its normal state, and letters out of their normal state are letters in a new order
indicatorNotes.mostly: mostly means most of it and not all, so the word named loses its last letter

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
cold without its final letter, the three that join the fodder

annotation.surface: A speech unusually short and chilly, and largely persuasive.
annotation.walkthrough: The indicator sits at the front and reaches over both pieces, so the docking happens before the shuffle. 'Brief, cold' reads as a description of a manner, which is how eight letters of fodder pass unnoticed.
annotation.definitionFit: A forcible argument carries force and so convinces; the adjective is about the strength that persuades, not about violence.

entries.clue: Describing acid quote upset Bill at first (6)

indicatorNotes.upset: upset is overturned, and in a down entry an overturned word is written from the bottom up
indicatorNotes.at first: at first says where a piece goes rather than what it is: those letters take the front of the answer

blocks.note: a bill is an account, written a/c on a statement
to quote is to cite, and those letters run the other way here

annotation.surface: An acid remark: a quotation that upset Bill from the very start.
annotation.walkthrough: A bill and an account are the same thing at the bank, which is why a/c does duty for both. 'At first' is a position, not a beheading — it says where the two letters go.
annotation.definitionFit: Acetic is the adjective belonging to vinegar's acid, so it describes an acid rather than naming one.

entries.clue: Fuel doesn’t last, hell inside! (6)

indicatorNotes.inside: the inside of a word is what is left standing when its outer letters are stripped off

blocks.note: what does not last dies
the two letters in the middle of that four-letter word

annotation.surface: Fuel running out, with hell in the middle of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells 'hell inside' as outrage, and it is an instruction. Rudolf Diesel gave his name to the engine and to the oil it burns.
annotation.definitionFit: Diesel is the heavy oil that runs lorries, trains and taxis, named after the engineer whose engine burns it.

entries.clue: Yorkshire racecourse manager, Harry (9)

blocks.note: a small flat and jumps course beside a garrison town in North Yorkshire
the man who took Everton to two league titles in the 1960s answered to that first name

annotation.surface: A Yorkshire racecourse and the Harry who runs it.
annotation.walkthrough: Harry Catterick's Everton won the league in 1963 and 1970, and he is one of only two men to manage them to a title since the war. The racecourse is in North Yorkshire, beside the army camp.
annotation.definitionFit: Catterick is both a North Yorkshire racing venue near the garrison and the surname of Harry Catterick, Everton's title-winning manager.

entries.clue: English opening contest (5)

blocks.note: e = English
a vent is an opening cut to let air through

annotation.surface: A tournament played with the English Opening.
annotation.walkthrough: The English Opening is a real chess move order, which is the whole of the surface. Athletics uses the answer for each separate contest within a meeting, which is the sense wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: An event is a single contest — the hundred metres is one event of the meeting — so the noun substitutes straight in.

entries.clue: Part of play getting noticed reportedly (5)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: reportedly means as reported aloud, so what counts is the sound of the word rather than its spelling

blocks.note: something getting noticed is being seen, and that sound is spelt another way here

annotation.surface: A part of a play that is, by all accounts, getting itself noticed.
annotation.walkthrough: A play divides into acts and then into scenes, so the definition is exact rather than loose. The two spellings sound identical and mean nothing like each other, which is all a homophone needs.
annotation.definitionFit: A scene is one division of an act in a play, the unit a stage direction names.

entries.clue: Time of charges for 1A, familiarly (7)

blocks.note: t = time
the word taken exactly as it stands
what a solicitor charges are fees

annotation.surface: The season of the year when the bills come in.
annotation.walkthrough: Everton are the Toffees after the toffee shops by the old ground, and sweets are still thrown to the crowd before kick-off. 'Familiarly' is the setter asking for a nickname.
annotation.definitionFit: The Toffees is Everton's nickname, taken from the toffee shops beside the ground, so 'familiarly' wants the fans' name rather than the club's.

entries.clue: Young prison reformer (3)

blocks.note: the collective word for newly hatched fish
the Quaker campaigner who exposed conditions in Newgate and later appeared on the five-pound note

annotation.surface: A young person who reformed the prisons.
annotation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Fry went into Newgate in 1813 and spent thirty years making Parliament look at what she found there. The fish sense has no singular: a river holds fry, never a fry.
annotation.definitionFit: Fry are the young of fish, small fry in the literal sense; and Fry is the surname of the reformer who changed Britain's prisons.

entries.clue: One of large group, many, at race, at the outset moving around (4,3)

indicatorNotes.at the outset: the outset of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter is taken
indicatorNotes.moving around: things moving around end up somewhere other than where they began, and so do these letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
the first letter of that word, joining the fodder

annotation.surface: One of a crowd at a race, milling about before the off.
annotation.walkthrough: Army ants march in columns of hundreds of thousands and bridge gaps with their own bodies, so 'large group' is no exaggeration. The fodder arrives in three separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: An army ant lives in a colony hundreds of thousands strong, so one of them is one of a very large group indeed.

entries.clue: I’m pleasantly surprised originally as help arrives (3)

indicatorNotes.originally: the origin of a word is its opening letter, so each word named gives up that and nothing else

blocks.note: the first letters of the three words, read in order

annotation.surface: Delight at the moment help finally turns up.
annotation.walkthrough: An exclamation is hard to define, so setters write out the feeling instead: a whole sentence stands in for a noise. Three short words in a row is the usual shape of an initials clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Aha is what you say when something welcome dawns on you, so the clue spells out the feeling the noise carries.

entries.clue: In front of Palace this could make rival of 1A? (7)

annotation.definition: In front of Palace this could make rival of 1A?

blocks.note: read as standing outside the gates of a royal residence, and meant as where the answer goes when the two words are written together
the pair names a south London club Everton meet twice a season, and the question mark concedes how loosely rival is being used

annotation.surface: Somebody standing in front of a palace who could turn into a rival.
annotation.walkthrough: There is no fodder to work on: the answer is simply the word that turns Palace into a football club. The question mark concedes that 'rival' covers any other team in the league.
annotation.definitionFit: Crystal Palace is a south London football club, so the answer is exactly the word that has to go in front of Palace to produce one of Everton's opponents.

entries.clue: Howard’s trick — ultimately close everything (7)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately points at the end of the word just named, which gives up its final letter alone

blocks.note: the last letter of that word
to close a meeting is to end it
everything is all of it

annotation.surface: Howard's last trick, closing everything down.
annotation.walkthrough: Howard Kendall played in Everton's 1970 title side and managed the 1985 and 1987 ones. 'Ultimately' takes a letter from the end of the word in front of it, not from the end of the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Howard Kendall won Everton two league titles in the 1980s, so in a grid full of Everton the forename on its own names the man.
